prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Despite the geologists’ knowledge and craft, mocking magnets, graphs, and maps— in a split second the dream piles before us mountains as stony as real life. And since mountains, then valleys, plains with perfect infrastructures. Without engineers, contractors, workers, bulldozers, diggers, or supplies— raging highways, instant bridges, thickly populated pop-up cities. Without directors, megaphones, and cameramen— crowds knowing exactly when to frighten us and when to vanish. Without architects deft in their craft, without carpenters, bricklayers, concrete pourers—on the path a sudden house just like a toy, and in it vast halls that echo with our steps and walls constructed out of solid air. Not just the scale, it’s also the precision—a specific watch, an entire fly, on the table a cloth with cross-stitched flowers, a bitten apple with teeth marks. And we—unlike circus acrobats, conjurers, wizards, and hypnotists— can fly unfledged, we light dark tunnels with our eyes, we wax eloquent in unknown tongues, talking not with just anyone, but with the dead. And as a bonus, despite our own freedom, the choices of our heart, our tastes, we’re swept away by amorous yearnings for—and the alarm clock rings. So what can they tell us, the writers of dream books,the scholars of oneiric signs and omens, the doctors with couches for analyses— if anything fits, it’s accidental, and for one reason only, that in our dreamings, in their shadowings and gleamings, in their multiplings, inconceivablings, in their haphazardings and widescatterings at times even a clear-cut meaning may slip through.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Despite, And, Without

outputs.L1:
Despite the geologists’ knowledge and craft—despite their magnets, graphs, and maps—in a split second the dream heaps before us mountains as stony as real life. And where there are mountains, there are valleys, plains with perfect infrastructures. Without engineers, contractors, workers, bulldozers, diggers, or supplies: raging highways, instant bridges, thickly populated pop-up cities. Without directors, megaphones, or cameramen: crowds that know exactly when to frighten us and when to vanish. Without architects deft in their craft, without carpenters, bricklayers, or concrete pourers: along the path, a sudden house, toy-like, and within it vast halls echoing with our steps, and walls constructed out of solid air.

It is not only a matter of scale, but also of precision: a specific watch, an entire fly, a cloth on the table embroidered with cross-stitched flowers, a bitten apple marked by teeth. And we—unlike circus acrobats, conjurers, wizards, and hypnotists—can fly unfledged; we light dark tunnels with our eyes; we wax eloquent in unknown tongues, speaking not merely with anyone, but with the dead. And, as a bonus, despite our own freedom, the choices of our hearts, and our tastes, we are swept away by amorous yearnings for—and then the alarm clock rings.

So what can they tell us, the writers of dream books, the scholars of oneiric signs and omens, the doctors with couches for analyses? If anything fits, it is accidental, and for one reason only: in our dreamings, in their shadowings and gleamings, in their multiplings, inconceivablings, haphazardings, and widescatterings, at times even a clear-cut meaning may slip through.
outputs.L2:
For all the expertise and skill of geologists, and in defiance of magnets, charts, and maps, a dream can, in an instant, heap up before us mountains as hard and convincing as those in waking life. And where there are mountains, there are also valleys, and plains equipped with flawless systems of roads and services. With no engineers, no contractors, no laborers, no bulldozers, excavators, or materials, there appear roaring highways, bridges built in a flash, and densely inhabited cities that spring up from nowhere. With no directors, no megaphones, and no camera crews, crowds understand precisely when to terrify us and when to disappear. With no skilled architects, no carpenters, masons, or workers pouring concrete, a house suddenly stands in our way like a toy, and inside it are enormous halls that resound under our footsteps, with walls made of solid air.

It is not only a matter of size, but of exactness: a particular watch, a complete fly, a tablecloth embroidered with cross-stitched flowers, an apple already bitten and bearing the marks of teeth. And we, unlike acrobats, illusionists, magicians, or hypnotists, can fly without wings, illuminate dark tunnels with our eyes, and speak fluently in languages we do not know—not merely to strangers, but to the dead. As an added gift, despite our freedom, our preferences, and the inclinations of our hearts, we are carried off by passionate longing for someone—and then the alarm clock sounds.

So what can the interpreters of dream books, the experts in dream symbols and omens, or the doctors with their analytic couches really tell us? If anything happens to match, it does so by chance, and only because in our dreams—with all their shadows and flashes, their multiplying forms, impossibilities, randomness, and wide dispersal—now and then even a distinct meaning may happen to pass through.
outputs.L3:
Dreams have the extraordinary ability to create entire worlds in an instant. Without any planning, labor, architecture, or conscious effort, the sleeping mind can produce vast landscapes, crowded cities, towering buildings, unfamiliar streets, and complex structures. What would require years of human work in waking life may appear fully formed in a dream, complete with movement, atmosphere, and a sense of reality.

The dream world is remarkable not only because of its scale, but also because of its detail. A dream may contain the texture of stone, the sound of footsteps, the faces of strangers, the layout of houses, the weather of a particular evening, or the shifting light of a strange sky. These details often feel precise and vivid while the dream is being experienced, as though the world has an independent existence beyond the dreamer’s mind.

Within this world, ordinary limits no longer apply. In dreams, people may fly without wings, see clearly in darkness, speak languages they do not know, or hold conversations with those who are dead. The impossible becomes natural, and events that would seem absurd in waking life are accepted without surprise. Dreams allow the mind to move beyond the laws of physics, memory, and ordinary experience.

At the same time, dreams can also dominate the dreamer’s sense of freedom. They may impose sudden emotions, fears, desires, or attachments that feel overwhelming and unquestionable. A person may be filled with terror, love, anger, or longing without choosing these feelings. The dream can push the dreamer through situations against personal preference or reason, only to end suddenly and completely when waking occurs.

For this reason, attempts to interpret dreams with certainty are unreliable. Dreams contain such a chaotic abundance of images, emotions, and events that any clear meaning found within them may be accidental rather than deliberate. Although a dream may seem symbolic or significant, its apparent message can easily arise from disorder, association, or chance. The richness of dreams makes them fascinating, but it also makes their interpretation uncertain.
outputs.L4:
Dreams reveal an astonishing creative power, one that seems to act without effort, hesitation, or plan. In sleep, the mind becomes a builder of impossible worlds. It raises palaces in an instant, stretches cities across the sky, opens abysses beneath familiar rooms, and fills empty space with crowds, landscapes, voices, music, and movement. What waking imagination might struggle to invent over many hours, the dream produces at once, complete in detail and charged with emotion. A street never seen before appears with every window, stone, shadow, and passerby already in place. A person long dead speaks naturally. A childhood house connects to a foreign country. A single door opens onto the sea, a mountain, or another century.

This power is not only creative but unpredictable. Dreams do not obey the rules that govern waking life. In them, one may see without eyes, hear distant conversations, understand unknown languages, or recognize people whose faces keep changing. The dreamer may fly, fall without landing, breathe underwater, speak with animals, become another person, or exist in several places at once. Time may rush forward, circle back, or disappear altogether. A few seconds of sleep can contain the events of years. Objects change their nature without surprise: a book becomes a bird, a room becomes a forest, a stranger is suddenly known to be a brother. The dream accepts contradictions that waking reason would reject immediately.

Desire also moves strangely through dreams. Wishes may appear openly, disguised, reversed, or broken into fragments. A longing for love may take the form of pursuit, a fear may appear as an invitation, and a memory may return wearing the mask of something entirely new. Dreams join together what has no obvious connection: yesterday’s conversation, an old anxiety, a bodily sensation, a forgotten image, and a sudden fantasy. They combine these materials freely, without concern for order or explanation. Their language is vivid, but it is not always logical.

For this reason, the interpretation of dreams is uncertain. It is tempting to treat every dream as a coded message and every image as a symbol with a fixed meaning. Yet dreams often scatter their meanings chaotically. They borrow from memory, sensation, fear, habit, and accident. A dream may seem profound simply because it is intense; it may appear symbolic when it is only a strange mixture of recent impressions. To explain every detail with confidence is usually to impose order where none may exist.

Still, this does not mean dreams are meaningless. At times, a dream may reveal a hidden worry, an unspoken wish, or a truth the waking mind has avoided. Occasionally, among the confusion, one clear meaning shines through. But such moments are exceptions rather than rules. Dreams are less like carefully written riddles than like storms of images, feelings, and associations. They can illuminate, but they can also mislead. Their wonder lies precisely in this mixture of invention and disorder: they are creations of the mind that astonish even the mind that creates them.
outputs.L5: Despite the challenges we face in life, we can still find the strength to move forward. Every day brings new opportunities, and each experience teaches us something valuable. Without courage, patience, and hope, it would be difficult to overcome obstacles. However, when we believe in ourselves and support one another, even the hardest moments can lead to growth and success.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about the impossible architecture and logic of dreams, in the style of Wisława Szymborska, ending with skepticism toward dream interpretation.
counterfactuals.output:
In dreams, the staircase remembers being a river and behaves accordingly.

It rises, but with a current. It carries shoes, childhoods, a spoon from a kitchen no longer standing. At the landing, a door opens into Tuesday, although the handle is clearly made of rain. Behind it, my grandmother is younger than I am and scolds a teapot for singing in a language we almost invented.

The rooms are numerous and poorly supervised. One contains a forest folded into a wardrobe. Another, a courtroom where the judge is a horse, very just, very tired. The ceiling has forgotten its duties and floats near the floor, which, out of politeness, pretends not to notice. Windows look inward. Mirrors reflect what will happen if I don’t wake up.

Nothing is impossible there, which is perhaps the first impossibility.

A dead friend arrives with a message, but first must find his pockets. A train departs from the bathtub. I am late for an exam in a subject called Being Myself, though I have attended all the lectures and even taken notes in disappearing ink. The questions are simple: Why this face? Why this fear? Show your work.

Dream logic is economical. It wastes no time explaining why the moon fits in a drawer, why a stranger knows my name, why I can run and remain in place like a flag in a windless country. It simply declares: therefore. And the soul, that gullible bureaucrat, stamps the papers.

By morning the architecture collapses without a sound. The staircase is again only stairs, innocent of rivers. The teapot denies everything. My dead friend keeps his message, if he had one.

Then come the interpreters with their little lamps and their confident keys. This means desire, they say. That means dread. The horse is your father. The train is transition. The bathtub, of course, is the womb.

Perhaps.

But I have seen a ceiling refuse the sky, and a spoon cross an ocean to return to an empty drawer.

I would not trust a key  
that opens every door.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free-verse poem that marvels at how dreams create mountains, cities, objects, languages, flight, and encounters with the dead without any real-world labor or planning.
counterfactuals.output:
In sleep, no quarryman lifts a hammer,  
yet mountains shoulder themselves from darkness,  
snow already thinking in silver  
on their impossible peaks.

No architect bends over a desk,  
no permit is signed, no scaffold raised—  
still a city arrives entire:  
alleys breathing rain, windows lit,  
a café where someone is always turning  
just as you enter.

A cup appears in your hand  
with the weight of a remembered morning.  
A red bicycle leans against a wall  
that did not exist a moment ago.  
The wall has ivy.  
The ivy has centuries.

And languages—  
how they bloom on the tongue,  
strange and understood,  
their grammar made of moonlight,  
their alphabets swimming like fish  
through air.

Then, without engine or wing,  
the body becomes an answer  
to a question gravity forgot.  
You rise over roofs, rivers, orchards,  
over the small blue fires of streetlamps,  
effortless as a thought  
escaping its cage.

Most wondrous of all,  
the dead come walking.

No grave is opened.  
No stone is moved.  
They arrive wearing their old coats,  
their voices warm with weather,  
offering bread, advice, laughter,  
or only the silence  
we were never able to keep with them.

All this made from nothing—  
no hand blistered,  
no blueprint smudged,  
no budget broken,  
no years spent learning the craft.

The dreaming mind, lavish and lawless,  
raises ranges, invents nations,  
coins tools, teaches tongues,  
loosens the earth from our feet,  
and seats us once more  
across from the lost,

as if creation  
were not work at all,  
but a door opening  
in the dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an English literary translation/adaptation of a Polish-style poem about dreams, emphasizing their instant construction, surreal precision, and resistance to psychoanalytic explanation.
counterfactuals.output:
**Dreams**

They build themselves at once—  
no scaffolding, no foreman,  
no bricklayer wiping lime from his hands.

A city appears, exact to the last keyhole,  
though no one has drawn its plans.  
The street knows where to turn.  
The door knows whom to refuse.  
A dead aunt is already waiting  
in a hat she never owned.

Everything is punctual there:  
the train departing from a meadow,  
the fish speaking with the voice of a judge,  
the moon folded neatly in a drawer.  
Even terror has clean edges.  
Even nonsense keeps appointments.

And afterward, the learned men arrive  
with their lamps and Latin,  
their small silver tools for opening symbols.  
They ask the staircase what it means.  
They question the horse, the flooded room,  
the child with my grandfather’s eyes.

But the dream says nothing.

It has no confession to make,  
no childhood hidden under the bed,  
no wish disguised as a crow.  
It was not a message—  
only a country, furnished in a second,  
where I lived without surprise  
until waking made it strange.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a philosophical poetic monologue praising the mind’s dream-making powers—its landscapes, crowds, houses, tiny details, and absurd emotions—then conclude that dream dictionaries can only be accidentally right.
counterfactuals.output:
O wondrous mind, nocturnal architect,  
you close the eyes and raise a continent.

With no stone, you build stairways that remember footsteps;  
with no sky, you hang weather over impossible fields.  
You summon cities from a pulse:  
streets twisting like sentences,  
windows lit by secrets,  
houses with too many rooms,  
rooms that open into childhood,  
childhood that opens into the sea.

Who taught you this art—  
to make a door feel guilty,  
to give a table the gravity of fate,  
to place one blue cup on a windowsill  
and make it seem more important than history?

You populate the dark with multitudes:  
old friends wearing the faces of strangers,  
the dead speaking casually by a vending machine,  
a teacher, a king, a woman selling oranges,  
a crowd that knows your name  
though you have never met them.  
You give them gestures, errands, grudges,  
pockets full of coins,  
shoes damp from rain that never fell.

And the details—ah, the details.  
A crack in plaster.  
A dog’s left ear.  
The smell of dust in a sunlit hall.  
A newspaper headline that cannot be reread.  
A spoon bent slightly at the handle.  
The tiny, faithful inventions  
by which unreality persuades us  
it has always been real.

Then come the emotions, absurd and sovereign:  
terror before a harmless curtain,  
grief for a misplaced hat,  
ecstasy because a staircase turns green,  
shame in front of a committee of birds.  
In dreams, feeling does not explain itself.  
It arrives crowned and unquestioned,  
declaring: this matters,  
and the sleeping soul obeys.

What philosopher can rival this?  
What painter, what dramatist, what god of small machinery?  
The mind, alone in its chamber,  
becomes world, witness, victim, and author.  
It hides the script from itself  
so it may gasp at its own inventions.

And yet, when morning comes,  
we drag these blazing fragments  
to the market stalls of interpretation.  
A snake means treachery, they say.  
A house means the self.  
Teeth mean anxiety.  
Water means change.

Perhaps. Sometimes. By accident.

For dreams are not a codebook written in symbols;  
they are weather in the soul,  
the mind thinking in thunder, furniture, faces, and flight.  
A dictionary may guess the rain from a puddle,  
may stumble upon truth as a drunkard finds the moon in a ditch—  
but if it is right, it is only accidentally right.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a Szymborska-inspired poem called “In Praise of Dreams,” with long cascading sentences, ironic comparisons to experts and craftsmen, and an ending about meaning appearing only by chance.
counterfactuals.output:
## In Praise of Dreams

In dreams I am promoted without documents,  
dismissed without scandal,  
summoned before a tribunal of clouds  
where the judges, being pillows,  
understand everything and therefore acquit me.

There I can repair the clock of my childhood  
with a spoon, a matchstick, and the advice of a dead aunt,  
while master watchmakers, bent over their bright instruments,  
would only clear their throats,  
consult Switzerland,  
and ask whether the parts were original.

In dreams the sea moves into my room  
without troubling the landlord,  
fish examine my books with professional disappointment,  
and a whale, that eminent scholar of depth,  
turns out to know less about sorrow  
than a cracked cup on the windowsill.

I speak fluent tiger,  
I negotiate with statues,  
I win an argument with a staircase  
that has spent its whole career going both up and down  
and still pretends to be neutral.

How generously dreams distribute competence:  
the butcher becomes an astronomer of ribs,  
the astronomer trims the moon like fat from meat,  
the tailor stitches a horizon to my sleeve  
and calls it ready-to-wear eternity,  
though any apprentice could see  
the seam is crooked,  
the blue thread borrowed,  
the measurements taken from someone already gone.

And the experts, poor experts,  
with their certificates polished like spectacles,  
arrive too late,  
carrying explanations in tidy boxes,  
while the dream has already changed addresses,  
married a bicycle,  
and left behind only one glove,  
one feather,  
one sentence beginning with “therefore”  
and ending in a field.

In dreams even death is badly trained,  
forgetting its lines,  
entering from the wrong side,  
wearing a hat too large for its authority,  
so that I almost feel sorry for it,  
as one feels sorry for a locksmith  
called to open a door  
that has decided to become a window.

O clumsy kingdom,  
O republic of misplaced keys and obedient monsters,  
where the impossible works overtime  
and the possible sleeps through its appointment,  
how can I not praise you  
when waking life, with all its clerks and carpenters,  
its engineers of consequence,  
its professors of because,  
builds such straight corridors  
to rooms we never meant to enter?

Still, I know:  
your wisdom is not wisdom,  
your prophecies are only laundry tossed by wind,  
your revelations wear shoes of different sizes.

If meaning appears there,  
it is not because someone planned it,  
not the architect, not the priest,  
not the ant with its admirable résumé,  
but because, for one second,  
among the falling hats, the speaking stones,  
the train departing from the kitchen table,  
something happens to land  
face up.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
